title: In 2005, a high-school student scanning free NASA–ESA images spotted one tiny dot beside the Sun; his report helped confirm a new sungrazing comet
byline: TOI Science Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Sep 24, 2026, 18:00 IST
excerpt: For most of history, spotting a new comet meant spending years at a telescope, often before dawn, waiting for a faint object to appear in the sky. In a lifetime, perhaps a handful of amateur astronomers and a small group of professional astronomers ever succeeded in this.
content:
AI-generated representative image showing a student examining solar-observatory images and spotting a tiny sungrazing comet near the Sun. Credits - Google Gemini

For most of history, spotting a new comet meant spending years at a telescope, often before dawn, waiting for a faint object to appear in the sky. In a lifetime, perhaps a handful of amateur astronomers and a small group of professional astronomers ever succeeded in this.

That changed when space agencies started posting their spacecraft photographs online for the public to see, making comet hunting available from a bedroom to almost anyone with a computer and a lot of patience.This trend has been driven by some of the missions which have monitored the sun for decades, such as the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, a cooperative project between NASA and the European Space Agency. Its cameras employ a disc to obscure the Sun's glare, allowing fainter objects nearby to be seen, including tiny sungrazing comets that go unseen by practically every other sensor on Earth or in space. A high school student, Quanzhi Ye, sorted through freely available photos from the observatory and found a minor sungrazing comet through a citizen science programme, a discovery that was later confirmed by NASA.A project developed for public engagementSo many people throughout the world were finding unlisted comets soon after the observatory began sending back photographs in 1996; mission scientists required a formal means to keep track of them all. In the early 2000s they launched a dedicated citizen science effort, the Sungrazer project, a NASA-funded programme that lets anyone with an internet connection sift through the spacecraft's images and report anything that looks like a comet.

The observatory was never actually planned to search for comets at all, and the response has been much above anything the original planners of the mission ever envisioned, the project's main investigator said.In 2005, Ye's report marked the project's 1,019th comet finding, a milestone that put him in the company of a growing community of school kids, pensioners and hobbyists throughout the world who had turned an afternoon of screen time into a real scientific contribution.

Most sungrazing comets are barely tens of metres across and do not survive their close pass by the Sun, making them impossible to observe from the ground, visible only by chance, through instruments that were never built to look for them.

His early achievement was not a fluke. He went on to report several more comets from the same platform before he even left school, developing the ability to spot the faint, slow-moving dots that distinguish a real finding from a passing satellite or a camera artefact.

Hubble Space Telescope images show Comet 9P/Tempel 1 before and after NASA’s Deep Impact spacecraft struck its surface on July 4, 2005, with the expanding plume of dust becoming increasingly prominent after the impact. Credits - science.nasa.gov

From school project to research careerYe studied planetary science at university, gaining his Bachelor of Science in China before completing a Master's and doctorate in astronomy at the University of Western Ontario in Canada, and undertaking postdoctoral research at the California Institute of Technology. His scholarly work has concentrated on the connections between meteor showers, comets and asteroids, the same family of minor solar system bodies he originally encountered as a teenager while poring over solar-observatory images.In 2023, the approach was formally honoured when Ye earned the Harold C. Urey Prize from the American Astronomical Society, awarded through its Division for Planetary Sciences for exceptional research early in his career. The citation noted his work on meteor showers, interstellar comets and near-Earth asteroids, and his public outreach in English and Chinese, a full circle moment for someone who previously discussed his comet discovery from a school computer lab.The citizen science project he previously utilised as a student has resulted in thousands of comet discoveries and launched several of its youngest volunteers into real careers in astronomy. But it's worth remembering the story for what it represents: that a piece of publicly financed space data freely available on the internet can sometimes give an average teenager a little but real place in the history of astronomy.

For a field traditionally associated with expensive telescopes and years of specialist training, that remains remarkable.
